claims.text: The corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily caused by a dense, chromium-enriched oxide layer.
The chromium-enriched oxide layer consists mainly of Cr2O3.
The Cr2O3-based layer forms rapidly and self-heals after damage.
The oxide layer acts as a physical barrier against the ingress of corrosive species.
A chromium content above approximately 10 wt% is sufficient to support corrosion resistance and native passivation in the proposed steels.
Minor additions of nickel and molybdenum are characteristic of the proposed corrosion-resistant steel.
Mechanical polishing removes the native passivating oxide layer.
A surface inhibitor can block reformation of the oxide layer.
Oxidizing species react with chromium at the steel surface to form Cr2O3.
The Cr2O3 layer limits diffusion of oxygen and chloride ions toward the underlying steel.
Limiting the transport of corrosive species impedes electrochemical corrosion reactions in the underlying steel.
Specimens retaining or rapidly reforming the oxide layer will have significantly lower corrosion rates than specimens in which film reformation is inhibited.
Spectroscopy and impedance measurements will show greater stability of the Cr2O3 film on uninhibited specimens than on inhibitor-treated specimens.
Untreated specimens will show quicker re-establishment of the Cr2O3 film than inhibited specimens.
The proposed mechanism should hold only for steels with enough chromium and environments representative of chemical-processing or nuclear-power service.
The mechanism may not hold outside 80–150 °C, at substantially different corrosive aggressiveness, or for alloy compositions that do not favor Cr2O3 formation.
The kinetics of oxide self-healing depend uncertainly on dynamic stresses and minor alloying elements.

contradictions.description: The untreated baseline is defined as retaining an intact native oxide, but the predicted outcome says that untreated samples will show quicker oxide 're-establishment.' An intact-film specimen should not require re-establishment unless a separate damage or stripping step is specified.

The oxide-stripped group is allowed to reform its film, yet the prediction and falsification rule sometimes describe film-removed samples as if they remain without a passivating oxide. Only the inhibitor-treated group is designed to maintain blocked reformation.
